record.original_question: Let G = An or Sn and let H, K be soluble subgroups of G. For all sufficiently large n, can we always find an element x ∈ G such that H ∩ K x = 1? Does this hold for all n ⩾ 21? Note that the conclusion is false when G = S20 and H = K = (S4 ≀ S4) × S4.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
For a positive integer $n$, let $S_n$ denote the symmetric group on $n$ letters and $A_n$ the alternating group. Recall that a finite group is soluble (solvable) if it has a subnormal series with abelian factors, and that for $x\in G$ and $K\le G$ we write $K^x = x^{-1}Kx$.

Let $G = A_n$ or $G = S_n$ and let $H, K$ be soluble subgroups of $G$.

(a) Is it true that for all sufficiently large $n$ there exists an element $x \in G$ such that 
$$H \cap K^x = 1?$$

(b) More precisely, does the conclusion in (a) hold for every $n \ge 21$?

(Note: when $n = 20$, $G = S_{20}$, and $H = K = (S_4 \wr S_4) \times S_4$ embedded in $S_{20}$, no such element $x$ exists, so the bound $n\ge 21$ would be sharp.)
